379.title: Chaupai close
379.hook: a short prayer for the times you feel unsafe
379.tomorrow: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
379.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib in the morning Nitnem and within the evening Rehras, and many also say it at night, before travel or in times of fear; Kirtan Sohila is the bani usually said before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, duaar, the last couplet, and your line, your door. Today, the whole Chaupai, and where it lives.

It's late. The lights are off, the house has gone quiet, and that's exactly when the mind gets loud. The thing someone said at work. The test results that aren't back. The noise outside that's probably nothing. Night makes every worry bigger. Some people turn on a podcast. Some scroll. Many Sikhs say a short prayer they know by heart, and for some, the one they reach for in the dark is the one you've spent ten days with.
screen: `LATE, LIGHTS OFF, MIND LOUD.` → `NIGHT MAKES WORRY BIGGER.` → `A PRAYER KNOWN BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Lay the prayer out end to end. A humble request, benti, in four-part verse. Protect me, giving me your hand. May my heart's wish be fulfilled, and my mind rest at your feet. End the enemies, outside, and for many Sikhs, inside: the five thieves. Carry my servants and Sikhs across the river. Then the prayer looks up: the Creator spreads creation out and gathers it in, knows every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad. Then, charan: since I held your feet, I look to no one else. And at last, leaving every other duaar, I have come to yours; Gobind is your servant. Ten days, one prayer, one movement: keep me. Where does it live in a Sikh day? In the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. In the evening, inside Rehras, the prayer said at dusk. At the amrit ceremony, recited as the water is stirred. And for some Sikhs, in the unscheduled moments too: before a long drive, at a hospital bedside, on a plane, in the dark. Ahead on this path you'll meet Kirtan Sohila, the bani many Sikhs say last thing at night. Chaupai isn't a replacement for that. It's more like the pocket prayer, the one that fits in the gaps: short, personal, asking for something very basic. And it was written by someone who knew real danger, so it never pretends danger isn't real. It just asks, in the middle of it, to be kept.
screen: `HAND, HEART, ENEMIES, THE RIVER.` · `SPREADS, GATHERS, KNOWS THE PAIN.` · `THE FEET, THEN THE DOOR.` · `MORNING, DUSK, AND THE GAPS.` · then, large: `KEEP ME.`

segments.voice: Choose the line from Chaupai you'd want in the dark: the hand, the heart's wish, he knows the pain, or every other door. Say it slowly a few times, in the original if you can, in English if you can't, breathing between, until it starts to feel familiar. If you pray, you can join it to Waheguru.

Chaupai Sahib, the Tenth Guru's prayer for protection. Ten days with it: the hand, the heart's wish, the enemies, the river, the knower of hearts, the feet and the door, folded into two words: keep me.
Your line: keep me. Two words, small enough to carry into the dark. Ten days of Chaupai, done.

screen: `DAY 379 COUNTS.` → `CHAUPAI, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: ANAND SAHIB: THE SONG OF BLISS.`

380.title: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
380.hook: forty pauris of joy found through the Guru, closing every Sikh gathering
380.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the first five pauris with the fortieth are sung at the close of nearly every Sikh service and ceremony, before the Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai Sahib closed, and your line was keep me. Now a new bani begins, the one Sikhs sing together.

At a Sikh wedding, the couple walks slowly around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four verses called the Laavan are sung. Then the music shifts. Before the final prayer, the whole room joins in a song: grandparents, cousins, friends who flew in, kids who've been fidgeting for an hour. The same song closes the ordinary Sunday service, a baby's naming, and a funeral. And the wedding shares its first word: the ceremony is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss.
screen: `FOUR ROUNDS, THE LAAVAN SUNG.` → `THEN THE WHOLE ROOM SINGS.` → `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Anand means bliss, a deep, settled joy. Anand Sahib is a bani by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, in Raag Ramkali, set in the Guru Granth Sahib: forty pauris, forty stanzas. You first met it on day one hundred thirty-three; now comes the slow walk through it, the way the Japji and Chaupai went. Two forms matter. Many Sikhs say all forty pauris in the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. And a short form, the first five pauris and the last, six in all, closes nearly every Sikh gathering, followed by the Ardas. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Amar Das composed it when a grandson was born to his family, and the child was named Anand. Whether or not every detail is exact, the story fits: this song comes out of a family's joy. And it's rarely a solo. It's the song a room sings. A wedding sings it on the way into a marriage; a funeral sings it on the way through grief. The same words, in both rooms. That says something about anand in this tradition. It isn't the high of a good day. It's a joy deep enough to be sung beside a coffin as well as beside a bride, a joy that can hold sorrow without breaking. And it's found, the song will say, through the Guru.
screen: `ANAND: DEEP, SETTLED JOY.` · `FORTY PAURIS; SIX CLOSE EVERY GATHERING.` · `BORN, TRADITION SAYS, OF A FAMILY'S JOY.` · `SUNG AT WEDDINGS AND FUNERALS ALIKE.` · then, large: `BLISS, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of the short Anand Sahib, the six pauris sung at the close of a Sikh service; it takes only a few minutes. Don't work at the words yet; just breathe with the sound of many voices singing one thing. If you can't play it now, picture a room full of people you love singing together, and if you pray, join with Waheguru at the end.
Anand. Bliss, a deep and settled joy; Guru Amar Das's forty-pauri song, whose six pauris close nearly every Sikh gathering, weddings and funerals alike.
Your line: bliss, together. Six pauris, many voices, and one song between them. Day three hundred eighty.

381.title: Pauri 1, sound: anand bhaiaa
381.hook: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa
381.howItsDone: Many Sikhs learn the opening of Anand Sahib by ear in childhood, singing it at the close of services; in kirtan it is sung in Raag Ramkali or in simpler congregational tunes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, the song of bliss, and your line, bliss, together. Today, the very first line, just its sound.

A song can get into a person long before they understand a word of it. A lullaby in a language you don't speak. A chant at a stadium. The first bars of a tune your grandmother hummed in the kitchen. The sound arrives first, and the meaning catches up later, sometimes years later. Plenty of Sikh kids can sing the opening of Anand Sahib long before anyone explains it to them. So today, before a single word of meaning, just the sound.
screen: `A SONG GETS IN BEFORE THE WORDS.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING LATER.` → `TODAY, JUST THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, transliterated: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa. Walk through its sounds. Anand, stress on the second syllable: a-NUND. Bhaiaa: bha-I-aa, three soft beats; it means has happened, has come. Meree maae: MAY-ree MAA-ay, my mother, a call, the way you'd call to someone in the next room. Then satguroo: sat-GU-roo, the True Guru. Mai: me, I. Paaiaa: PAA-i-aa, have found. Hear the music in it. Bhaiaa in the middle, paaiaa at the end: the line rhymes with itself, and the long aa sounds keep opening, like a mouth that's singing rather than speaking. It's written in a raag, Ramkali, to be sung. Its last line comes back almost to the start: kahai Naanak anand hoaa, satguroo mai paaiaa. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. The circle closes on the sound it opened with, and every pauri of Anand Sahib ends with kahai Naanak, says Nanak. One more detail. Guru Amar Das wrote this, not Guru Nanak. But in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Gurus who wrote after Guru Nanak sign their verses with his name. The Granth marks the writer with a number, Mahala three for Guru Amar Das, but the name in the verse is always Nanak. Sikhs understand that as one light passing from Guru to Guru: words of the third Guru, signed with the name of the first.
screen: `A-NUND BHA-I-AA MAY-REE MAA-AY.` · `BHAIAA AND PAAIAA: IT RHYMES.` · `EVERY PAURI ENDS: KAHAI NAANAK.` · `THE THIRD GURU SIGNS AS NANAK.` · then, large: `ANAND BHAIAA.`

segments.voice: Breathe in, and on the out-breath say it slowly: anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa, letting the long aa sounds open; it doesn't need to be perfect. Say it once more, and if you like, let it tip into a tune, or just repeat the first two words, anand bhaiaa, softly. If you pray, follow it with Waheguru, then sit in the quiet after the sound.
Satguroo, the True Guru. The opening of Anand Sahib, learned by sound: anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa, with every pauri ending kahai Naanak.
Your line: anand bhaiaa. Joy has come, in a sound small enough to hum. See you tomorrow.

382.title: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother
382.hook: joy, mother, I have found the True Guru, easily, and the songs of joy are sung (Anand 1)
382.tomorrow: Stay with the Lord, my mind
382.howItsDone: The first pauri of Anand Sahib is sung at the close of Sikh gatherings, from weddings to ordinary services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri one, satguroo, and your line, anand bhaiaa. Today, the same pauri, opened up for its meaning.

A baby is born in a Punjabi family, and within the hour the phone is ringing. Then the doorbell. Aunties arrive with sweets. Uncles arrive with more sweets. Someone puts music on. Everyone keeps saying one word to the parents, the grandparents, anyone standing still long enough: vadhaiyan! Congratulations! It's the word for news so good the whole family turns up. The first pauri of Anand Sahib has that word in it: a party in five lines, and the guests are not who you'd expect.
screen: `A BABY IS BORN; THE PHONE RINGS.` → `AUNTIES, SWEETS, MUSIC.` → `VADHAIYAN! CONGRATULATIONS!`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri, in paraphrase. Joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. I found the True Guru with ease, and my mind rings with congratulations. The jewel-like ragas, with their families, have come to sing the Word. Sing the Word of the Lord, all you who have set it in your minds. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. Take the pieces. First, mother: the news goes to the person you'd tell first. Then sahaj, with ease. Sahaj is a big word in Sikh thought: a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining. The Guru wasn't won by force; the joy came the way sleep comes. Then the party. Vaadhaaeeaa, congratulations, the same word aunties call out at a birth. And who shows up? The ragas. In old Indian music lore, ragas were pictured with families and companions, so the pauri pictures the musical modes themselves arriving at the door like relatives, ready to sing: joy so big the music turns up in person. Then a turn outward: sing the Word, all of you who've taken it in. The joy doesn't stay private. Notice what this pauri isn't. It isn't a lecture about joy. It's a report of joy, from inside it, still breathless. That's what Guru Amar Das gives Sikhs to sing at the close of their gatherings: not an idea about bliss, but good news.
screen: `JOY HAS COME, MY MOTHER.` · `SAHAJ: FOUND WITH EASE.` · `THE RAGAS ARRIVE LIKE FAMILY.` · `SING THE WORD, ALL OF YOU.` · then, large: `JOY, MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go over the last few days and find one piece of good news, any size: a friend's recovery, a finished project, a small win nobody noticed. Feel it again from inside, the way the pauri does, as news worth carrying to the first person you'd tell. If you pray, you can thank the Guru with Waheguru.
Sahaj, natural ease. Joy has come, my mother: the Guru found with sahaj, the mind ringing with congratulations, and the ragas arriving like family to sing.
Your line: joy, mother. Some news is too good to keep in one room. Three hundred eighty-two days, and counting.

383.title: Stay with the Lord, my mind
383.hook: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale: stay always with the Lord and your troubles will pass (Anand 2)
383.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this second pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and the opening line is often quoted as a reminder to keep the mind with God through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, and your line, joy, mother. Today, pauri two, where the Guru talks to his own mind.

Come on. Focus. Don't check the phone. You've got this. Plenty of people talk to themselves, even if they'd never admit it. Some of it is harsh, the inner voice that sounds like a bad coach. Some is kinder. Either way, the mind needs reminding, again and again, of what it already knows, because it wanders off the moment you stop watching. The second pauri of Anand Sahib is the Guru talking to his own mind. Not to a crowd. Not even to God, exactly. To himself.
screen: `EVERYONE TALKS TO THEMSELVES.` → `THE MIND NEEDS REMINDING.` → `THE GURU TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, transliterated: ae man meriaa too sadaa rahu har naale. O my mind, always stay with the Lord. Man is the mind, the restless inner self. Meriaa: my. Sadaa: always. Har naale: with the Lord, alongside. Then, in paraphrase: stay with the Lord, my mind, and all your pains will be forgotten. He will take you as his own, and set all your affairs right. The Master can do all things; why forget him from your mind? And it ends where it began: says Nanak, my mind, always stay with the Lord. Listen to the tone. It's not scolding. It's someone who has just found joy in pauri one, turning to his wandering mind and saying: stay. Don't drift off now. Naale is a lovely little word: beside, alongside, the word for walking with a friend. Not under, not far above. With. The promise is about the pains being forgotten, not about them never happening. The troubles are real; in the pauri, staying beside the Lord is what loosens their grip. Angeekaar, being taken as his own, is the idea you met in Chaupai: claimed, held, adopted. And then that gentle question, why forget him? Not a threat. Almost puzzled, the way you'd ask a friend who keeps wandering off from the one person who always shows up for them. The joy has come. Now the work is to stay with it.
screen: `AE MAN MERIAA: O MY MIND.` · `NAALE: ALONGSIDE, LIKE A FRIEND.` · `THE PAINS FORGOTTEN, NOT ABSENT.` · `WHY FORGET HIM? NOT A THREAT.` · then, large: `STAY WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple thing to stay with: your breath, the sound of a fan, or Waheguru if you pray. Every time the mind wanders off, and it will, bring it back gently, the way the pauri does, with no scolding: just, stay. Counting the returns can help.

Your line: stay with him. The mind wanders; the pauri keeps calling it back, kindly. Until tomorrow, then.

384.title: What your house doesn't hold
384.hook: true Master, what is there that is not in Your house (Anand, opening pauris)
384.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this third pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and its opening question is often quoted as an expression of trust and contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri two, man meriaa, and your line, stay with him. Today, pauri three asks a question about a house.

Some homes have a pantry that never seems to run out. A grandmother's kitchen where, no matter how many people turn up, there's always more: another pot of dal, another stack of rotis, a box of sweets from somewhere. You arrive hungry and leave carrying leftovers, and you never once wonder whether there'll be enough. Pauri three of Anand Sahib asks a question about a house like that, except the house is God's, and the question is almost a laugh of wonder.
screen: `A KITCHEN THAT NEVER RUNS OUT.` → `YOU LEAVE WITH LEFTOVERS.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT GOD'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the original: saachiaa saahibaa, kiaa naahee ghar terai. True Master, what isn't in your house? Then: everything is in your house. A question that answers itself. The pauri says that whoever keeps your praise always, and holds your Name in their mind, finds the music of the Word playing within. And it closes by asking again: says Nanak, true Master, what is not in your house? Two things make this more than a nice sentiment. First, ghar, house or home. In Sikh scripture, ghar often means more than a building: it's the inner home too, the self, the heart, where the Guru teaches the One is found. So the question works on two floors. Nothing is missing from God's house. And, the pauri hints, nothing is missing from the house within you, if the Name is living there. Second, who this is for. A lot of modern life runs on a quiet feeling of lack: not enough time, money, love, energy, success. Advertising depends on it. Pauri three meets that feeling with a question, not a list of what to want: look around the house. What isn't here? The pauri also says that each person receives what the Master gives; that line gets its own day soon. For today, just the wonder. The house is full.
screen: `TRUE MASTER, WHAT ISN'T IN YOUR HOUSE?` · `GHAR: HOUSE, AND THE HOME WITHIN.` · `THE QUIET FEELING OF LACK.` · `LOOK AROUND: WHAT IS MISSING?` · then, large: `NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: In your head, start a list of what's already in your house, and not just things: a roof, water from a tap, a person who'd answer if you called, your two hands, a memory you love. Keep going until the list is a little longer than you expected. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one; if not, let the size of it sink in.
Ghar terai, in your house. Pauri three: true Master, what is not in your house? Everything is there, and the same may be true of the home within.
Your line: nothing is missing. It comes as a question, so it can be asked again. Day three hundred eighty-four, done.

385.title: The Name my support
385.hook: the true Name is my support and satisfies every hunger (Anand, opening pauris)
385.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this fourth pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib at the close of services, and many remember the Name, saying Waheguru or a short prayer, before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghar terai, and your line, nothing is missing. This week: Chaupai closed with keep me, then Anand began: bliss together, anand bhaiaa, joy mother, stay with him, nothing is missing. Today, pauri four.

Ever eaten a whole meal and still felt hungry? Not stomach hungry. The other kind. You finish dinner and find yourself opening the fridge again, or scrolling for something to buy, or reaching for a phone with nothing new on it. There's a hunger food doesn't touch, and people feed it all day with whatever's nearest, and it never quite fills. The fourth pauri of Anand Sahib names something it says fills that hunger, all of it, with a word that also means what a building stands on.
screen: `A WHOLE MEAL, STILL HUNGRY.` → `THE FRIDGE, THE SCROLL, THE PHONE.` → `A HUNGER FOOD DOESN'T TOUCH.`

segments.voice: The pauri begins and ends with one line: saachaa naam meraa aadhaaro. The true Name is my support. Aadhaar means support, foundation, the base a thing rests on; the same word names India's national identity number today. In the pauri it's the ground under your feet. Then, in paraphrase: it has taken away all my hunger. It brought peace and calm to live in my mind, and fulfilled all my longings. I am forever a sacrifice to the Guru, who gives such greatness. Says Nanak, listen, saints: love the Word. Three things to notice. First, hunger. Bhukh is the plain everyday word, the hunger before lunch, and the pauri says the Name takes away all of it: a bold claim, made from experience, not as theory. Second, the order. Support first, then hunger gone, then peace comes to live in the mind. Peace isn't chased; it moves in once the foundation is there. Third, kurbaan, sacrifice: to give yourself wholly, the word people use when they'd do anything for someone. The joy of the first three pauris turns here into gratitude so full it wants to give itself away. And the pauri doesn't tell you to stop eating or stop wanting. It describes what happens when the deepest hunger is met: the smaller hungers lose their power. You're fed underneath.
screen: `AADHAAR: SUPPORT, FOUNDATION.` · `THE NAME TAKES AWAY ALL HUNGER.` · `THEN PEACE MOVES INTO THE MIND.` · `KURBAAN: GRATITUDE THAT GIVES ITSELF.` · then, large: `MY SUPPORT.`

segments.voice: If there's something to eat nearby, a piece of fruit or a sip of tea, take one bite now, or keep this for your next meal. Taste it fully, chew slowly, and notice the moment your body says, that's good. If you pray, you can say Waheguru first, the way many Sikhs remember the Name before eating; if not, just let the bite be enough.
Aadhaar, support or foundation. Saachaa naam meraa aadhaaro: the true Name is my foundation, and it takes away all hunger, so peace can come and live in the mind.
Your line: my support. A foundation holds up the whole house without being seen. That's day three hundred eighty-five.
